title: Shopping & Bargaining
description: Markets, stalls and shops: asking the price, bargaining with a smile, sizes and colours, and paying by card or QRIS. Call a stallholder Bu or Pak, or Mbak and Mas if they're young.

phrases.registerNotes: Point as you ask. Berapa harganya? (How much is it?) is the fuller version; say Pak to a man, and Mbak or Mas to someone young.

phrases.english: Could you go a bit lower?
phrases.registerNotes: The usual way to open bargaining, literally 'may it be less?'. Bisa kurang? means the same, and Kurang sedikit, ya? (a little less?) is softer still.
phrases.cultureNote: Bargaining is normal at markets, street stalls and souvenir shops, done with a smile. Printed prices, as in supermarkets, minimarkets and malls, are fixed.

phrases.registerNotes: Part of the bargaining routine, said lightly and with a smile rather than as a complaint. Terlalu mahal (too expensive) is blunter.

phrases.english: Would you take a hundred thousand?
phrases.registerNotes: Kalau (if) plus your price is the usual way to make an offer. Prices are said in thousands of rupiah: lima puluh ribu, seratus ribu.
phrases.cultureNote: Start well below the first price and expect to meet somewhere in between. Keep it friendly: a few thousand rupiah means more to the seller than to you.

phrases.registerNotes: Asks for the real price straight away. If the seller says Sudah harga pas (That's the fixed price), there's no more room to bargain.
phrases.pitfallNote: Harga pas (the fixed price) isn't uang pas, which is the exact change.

phrases.registerNotes: The friendly answer when a seller calls out Cari apa? (What are you looking for?). Saying lihat twice makes it relaxed browsing.

phrases.english: Do you have a bigger size?
phrases.registerNotes: Lebih kecil is smaller. Local clothes sizes tend to run small, so a New Zealand medium may be an L or XL here.
phrases.pitfallNote: There's no -er ending: bigger is lebih besar (more big), cheaper is lebih murah.

phrases.english: Do you have it in another colour?
phrases.registerNotes: Name the colour if you have one in mind: Ada yang hitam? (Do you have a black one?)
For clothes and shoes, and at a market for tasting the fruit too. The fitting room is the kamar pas.
Ambil (take) is how you say you'll buy it, in a shop or at the end of bargaining.
phrases.cultureNote: Once you've agreed a price, it's polite to buy. Walking away after the seller has said yes is bad form, so only bargain for something you want.

phrases.registerNotes: Markets, warungs and small shops are usually cash only (tunai), so carry small notes.

phrases.cultureNote: QRIS is Indonesia's national payment QR code, on a printed sign at most counters and many stalls. Visitors usually need an Indonesian e-wallet or banking app to use it, so carry cash too.

phrases.registerNotes: Kresek is the everyday word for a thin plastic bag.
phrases.cultureNote: Bali, Jakarta and many other places have banned single-use plastic bags in shops, so carry your own shopping bag (tas belanja).
